## 971 2022: a deliberate West Coast drive simplicity choice

Version: 971 2022 catapult robot. [PDF p3](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1RrrDPh5zAsCcHDBvC_XfE8EIunZshhFn/view?usp=sharing#page=3) · [PDF p5](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1RrrDPh5zAsCcHDBvC_XfE8EIunZshhFn/view?usp=sharing#page=5)

**Published construction:** Six Colson-wheel West Coast drive; two dual-Falcon gearboxes; 8:70 gearbox tooth ratio.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Robustness, low maintenance and short-distance acceleration.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A differential drive sacrifices direct sideways motion while reducing the number of independent drive and steering mechanisms. That trade can fit a robot whose turret provides aiming independence and whose collectors support acquisition from opposite sides. Wheel choice affects maintenance and turning losses as well as traction. The team’s post-COVID experience constraint is part of this architecture decision: the most sophisticated available module is not automatically the strongest choice when integration and practice capacity differ. Preserve the resource assumption rather than presenting a universal drivetrain ranking.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure short-cycle path time, turning current and defended maneuverability using the actual collector and turret operating policy.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## 971 2022: center and guide cargo rather than only gripping harder

Version: 971 2022 catapult robot. [PDF p6](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1RrrDPh5zAsCcHDBvC_XfE8EIunZshhFn/view?usp=sharing#page=6)

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Use known intake behavior and improve transfer support.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The pickup must establish both ownership and a useful lateral position for the catapult transfer. Mecanum contact supplies centering while the compliant arm accommodates shape and pressure variation. Additional upper rollers address the transition after the initial capture, where a ball can lose support or arrive at the receiver at an uncontrolled height. The lesson is to diagnose the entire handoff path: improving the first roller’s grip cannot solve a downstream gap that lets cargo escape.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Track the ball center through acquisition and transfer with several inflation states; test off-center pickup at realistic driving speed.

title: 971 2022: flippy arms combine retention and release
text:
## 971 2022: flippy arms combine retention and release

Version: 971 2022 catapult robot. [PDF p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1RrrDPh5zAsCcHDBvC_XfE8EIunZshhFn/view?usp=sharing#page=8)

**Published construction:** Spring-loaded paired transfer arms; one-way-bearing action opens them when rollers reverse.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Hold cargo in the catapult, then release it for firing.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The transfer mechanism serves as a timed constraint on the projectile. It must hold the cargo through turret alignment but stop exerting an unwanted force at release. Coupling reversal to opening reduces an actuator but creates a mechanical timing relationship that software must understand. Spring force and ball compression affect both retention and release delay. If the catapult controller assumes the ball is free before the arms actually clear, a perfectly tracked motor trajectory can still produce a poor shot.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure arm clearance and ball release timing relative to motor command, over cargo pressure and spring-wear variation.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: 971 2022: a controlled catapult instead of a flywheel

## 971 2022: a controlled catapult instead of a flywheel

Version: 971 2022 catapult robot. [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1RrrDPh5zAsCcHDBvC_XfE8EIunZshhFn/view?usp=sharing#page=9) · [PDF p13](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1RrrDPh5zAsCcHDBvC_XfE8EIunZshhFn/view?usp=sharing#page=13)

**Published construction:** Light carbon catapult, two Falcons, 7:99 tooth ratio and model-predictive launch control.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Team prototypes favored tolerance to cargo pressure and surface-friction variation.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A motor-driven catapult sets the projectile’s velocity through the motion of a supporting arm rather than relying primarily on slip against a high-speed wheel. That can reduce one source of friction sensitivity while introducing trajectory tracking, release timing and structural stiffness requirements. A lighter arm spends less energy accelerating itself and leaves more actuator authority for the cargo. The controller needs the correct state at release, not merely a final position, because angle and velocity together determine the shot. This is a specific tested alternative, not a claim that catapults universally beat flywheels.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure release angle and velocity across inflation and surface variation, compare with the flywheel prototype under equal conditions, and test mis-timed retention release.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: 971 2022: turret structure must also react climbing loads
text:
## 971 2022: turret structure must also react climbing loads

Version: 971 2022 catapult robot. [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1RrrDPh5zAsCcHDBvC_XfE8EIunZshhFn/view?usp=sharing#page=7) · [PDF p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1RrrDPh5zAsCcHDBvC_XfE8EIunZshhFn/view?usp=sharing#page=10)

**Published construction:** Turret carries catapult and climber; paired bearing support; climber revisions progress toward a spring-extended high-bar package.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Support firing and hanging loads with compact packaging.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A bearing sized only for smooth aiming may be inadequate once the suspended robot applies an overturning moment through the turret. Two support locations can define a load path for that moment while maintaining axis alignment. Shared structure saves space but couples the climber’s strength requirements to the shooter’s pointing stiffness. The documented objective changed from a mid-rung solution toward higher reach, so do not infer traversal capability from a general “climber” label. Each pictured prototype also needs its own competition-use evidence.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Check bearing and mount loads through firing and hanging, verify output-axis alignment afterward, and establish the dated competed climb configuration.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

text:
## ECHO: compliant vector pickup and cone centering

Version: ECHO. [PDF p8](https://773cbb55-5509-49bc-8d49-05aa4e1c4c70.filesusr.com/ugd/209e0c_40103d44bfcb4b2b877c4b14bb9d1563.pdf#page=8)

**Published construction:** Sponge/noodle roller, dustpan, powered centering flappers and bent-polycarbonate structure.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** The binder lists construction; detailed comparative selection reasoning is not supplied.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A broad soft contact can accommodate variation in approach and distribute pressure on a deformable piece. The dustpan supplies support underneath, while the flappers create a separate centering action. That is a different mechanism from merely adding compliant wheels to an arm. The soft material’s wear and compression set can alter intake behavior over an event; the structure must remain aligned while yielding to impacts. Because the binder does not give a complete rejected-alternatives account, these are engineering implications rather than a claim about the team’s exact selection process.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure centering success across cone orientations and roller wear, and inspect whether the dustpan or flappers create an escape path.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## ECHO: lightweight telescoping arm and roller end effector

Version: ECHO. [PDF p7](https://773cbb55-5509-49bc-8d49-05aa4e1c4c70.filesusr.com/ugd/209e0c_40103d44bfcb4b2b877c4b14bb9d1563.pdf#page=7) · [PDF p10](https://773cbb55-5509-49bc-8d49-05aa4e1c4c70.filesusr.com/ugd/209e0c_40103d44bfcb4b2b877c4b14bb9d1563.pdf#page=10)

**Published construction:** Sheet-metal pivot structure, carbon telescope, shimmed hex interfaces and light dead-axle end rollers.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Weight and backlash reduction are explicitly documented.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Reducing distal mass improves both arm acceleration and the chassis stability needed to exploit it. A light telescoping tube still needs sufficient overlap and guidance to resist bending and torsion at full extension. Shimmed interfaces target lost motion, while structure and belt elasticity remain separate error sources. Dead-axle rollers can remove rotating shaft mass and simplify the wheel assembly, but their supports must retain alignment. A recommendation should compare endpoint settling and piece ownership under load rather than claiming a material alone makes the arm fast.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure endpoint deflection at full reach and after reversing both axes; inspect telescoping guidance and roller support wear.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

That can lift a robot while changing its attitude without another actuator, but the force and mechanical advantage vary through the stroke. Over-center deployment can hold a state mechanically, while the ratchet provides a separate release/retention function. Partner geometry and platform angle determine the contact loads. The design should be retrieved as an alliance-specific balance solution rather than grouped indiscriminately with climbers from other seasons.

## ECHO: preload catapult and vacuum swiper are distinct tactical tools

Version: ECHO. [PDF p11](https://773cbb55-5509-49bc-8d49-05aa4e1c4c70.filesusr.com/ugd/209e0c_40103d44bfcb4b2b877c4b14bb9d1563.pdf#page=11) · [PDF p12](https://773cbb55-5509-49bc-8d49-05aa4e1c4c70.filesusr.com/ugd/209e0c_40103d44bfcb4b2b877c4b14bb9d1563.pdf#page=12)

**Published construction:** Spring-released one-shot cube catapult; dual vacuum cups added in a three-day development period.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Preload launch and opponent loading-zone cube acquisition.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A one-shot mechanism can be mechanically simpler than forcing the main manipulator to execute the same autonomous action, but it spends mass on a narrow use. Its value depends on repeatability and the time it frees for the rest of the routine. Vacuum acquisition relies on seal area, surface condition and resistance to peeling; it is poorly described by a generic grip-force number. The swiper is a dated tactical addition, not proof every earlier robot revision carried it. Keep the development date and task boundary attached to the feature.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test preload release over the allowed setup variation and vacuum retention under peeling loads and imperfect cube surfaces.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: OPR 2023: low-backlash articulated arm
text:
## OPR 2023: low-backlash articulated arm

Version: 2023 articulated arm. [PDF p9](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/2023_Tech_Binder_OPR2056.pdf#page=9) · [PDF p11](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/2023_Tech_Binder_OPR2056.pdf#page=11) · [PDF p13](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/2023_Tech_Binder_OPR2056.pdf#page=13)

**Published construction:** Two driven joints, dead axles, bronze bushings and gas-shock shoulder counterbalance.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Fast repeatable motion with motor-side position sensing.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** An articulated arm can reach floor, station and grid positions without a tall lift, but the endpoint error combines both joint errors. A small shoulder angle error becomes a larger tip error as the arm extends. Reducing backlash at shafts, gears and chains supports motor-side sensing only if elastic deformation remains acceptable. Gas shocks reduce gravitational torque over part of the motion but produce a changing torque with angle. A bronze bushing can be appropriate for high load and limited rotation, while friction and wear must be included in control tuning.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure tip repeatability approaching the same pose from both directions, under load and after chain wear.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: OPR 2023: piece-specific active contacts
text:
## OPR 2023: piece-specific active contacts

Version: 2023 articulated arm. [PDF p15](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/2023_Tech_Binder_OPR2056.pdf#page=15) · [PDF p16](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/2023_Tech_Binder_OPR2056.pdf#page=16)

**Published construction:** Pneumatic top roller for cubes, synchronized side rollers for cones and piece-specific sensors.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Center and hold both pieces while limiting damage.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The top roller and side pinch solve different shapes rather than forcing both through one fixed gap. Timing the side mechanism prevents one arm closing first and pushing the cone away. A sensor that reliably detects a cube may not see a cone in the same position, which explains why sensing belongs in the physical design. The control should stop or change the roller command after capture to avoid damaging the soft piece. Compliance reduces impact severity but must not let the frame spread enough to lose the intended contact geometry.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test skewed cone entry, cube retention during traversal and sensor-triggered transitions with worn or deformed pieces.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: OPR 2023: base mass supports arm motion
text:
## OPR 2023: base mass supports arm motion

Version: 2023 articulated arm. [PDF p5](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/2023_Tech_Binder_OPR2056.pdf#page=5) · [PDF p7](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/2023_Tech_Binder_OPR2056.pdf#page=7)

**Published construction:** Low Mk4i base; rear steel ballast and solid bellypan; rigid tower and dead-axle shoulder support.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Stable traversal and a stiff arm reference.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A lightweight arm does not eliminate its overturning moment. Low ballast and a broad support polygon can permit more aggressive joint motion, while adding driving load and stopping energy. Tower deflection appears as arm error even when both joint encoders are exact. The base, tower and arm should therefore be tested as one structure. The appropriate ballast location depends on the arm’s range and battery placement rather than a generic preference for more robot weight.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure wheel unloading and tool-tip motion during combined driving and arm transitions over cable track and platform edges.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: BREAKDOWN: independent vertical and lateral extension
text:
## BREAKDOWN: independent vertical and lateral extension

Version: BREAKDOWN. [PDF p12](https://media.team254.com/2023/10/90bc07c6-2023-Tech-Binder-V6.pdf#page=12) · [PDF p13](https://media.team254.com/2023/10/90bc07c6-2023-Tech-Binder-V6.pdf#page=13)

**Published construction:** Vertical elevator plus 15° inclined three-stage carbon-fiber laterator; PEEK guidance rollers.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Fast reach with low moving mass.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Separating vertical and outward motion turns scoring poses into two mostly independent coordinates. That can simplify the end-effector geometry and let the chassis remain farther from the grid, but adds another flexible stage and a collision envelope between stages. Low-mass carbon structures reduce inertia; guidance roller preload and tube alignment determine whether they move freely without excessive play. The laterator’s angle contributes vertical motion as it extends, so the control system still needs a coupled pose model. A reported travel time describes one axis, not a complete pickup-to-placement transition.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure coral-equivalent tool-tip error under simultaneous axis motion and chassis acceleration; inspect guidance play and cable drag across the entire stroke.

**Limits:** The PDF required OCR. Page 12 elevator construction was checked visually; other numerical OCR details should be checked in the original before fabrication.

title: BREAKDOWN: articulate contacts for cones and cubes
text:
## BREAKDOWN: articulate contacts for cones and cubes

Version: BREAKDOWN. [PDF p8](https://media.team254.com/2023/10/90bc07c6-2023-Tech-Binder-V6.pdf#page=8) · [PDF p15](https://media.team254.com/2023/10/90bc07c6-2023-Tech-Binder-V6.pdf#page=15)

**Published construction:** Articulating roller claw with distinct cube and cone contacts; over-center cone grip.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Serve upright cones and cubes without pursuing every floor orientation.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A cone and a cube present different contact and centering problems. An articulated claw can open enough for a cube while using a different smaller contact to constrain a cone. Over-center geometry can supply retention without continuous high motor force, provided the piece is located in the intended three-point contact. Choosing not to solve sideways floor cones is an explicit scope decision linked to expected high-level supply; it must not become a universal claim that such pickup has no value. A local event or a disrupted supply plan can change that assumption.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test each intended piece orientation and define a safe fallback for excluded orientations; measure grip after approach collisions.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: BREAKDOWN: rack-deployed cube floor pickup
text:
## BREAKDOWN: rack-deployed cube floor pickup

Version: BREAKDOWN. [PDF p16](https://media.team254.com/2023/10/90bc07c6-2023-Tech-Binder-V6.pdf#page=16)

**Published construction:** Rack-and-pinion polycarbonate extension and a small grippy roller feed the main claw.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Lightweight, robust access to floor cubes.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Linear extension preserves roller height while changing its distance from the chassis, which is useful when a simple pivot would change the pickup geometry too much. A rack cut directly into the side plate reduces part count but concentrates wear and impact load in that plate. The floor mechanism does not solve every piece task; it supplies a known cube path to the articulating claw. That specialization can be efficient when the human-player and game-piece plan makes it sufficient.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test cube acquisition near walls and with oblique contact; inspect rack alignment and tooth wear after repeated forced retractions.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: BREAKDOWN: forks change the robot’s balance interface
text:
## BREAKDOWN: forks change the robot’s balance interface

Version: BREAKDOWN. [PDF p17](https://media.team254.com/2023/10/90bc07c6-2023-Tech-Binder-V6.pdf#page=17)

**Published construction:** Carbon-fiber forks and a sliding carriage react against bumper structure; rope lift.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Lift alongside partners and balance quickly.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The forks are an alliance interaction mechanism. Their usefulness depends on the partner’s underside, bumper placement and where the combined load settles on the platform. Reacting through bumper wood can counter sag but creates a load path that needs appropriate mounting and repeatability. A mechanism that works under one partner may interfere with another, so compatibility belongs in the selection criteria. This differs fundamentally from a cage or rung climb despite sharing motors, rope and lifting motion.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test with representative partner geometries, unequal loading and platform tilt; verify the load path through the bumper attachment.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: BREAKDOWN: collision avoidance and compliant station intake
text:
## BREAKDOWN: collision avoidance and compliant station intake

Version: BREAKDOWN. [PDF p20](https://media.team254.com/2023/10/90bc07c6-2023-Tech-Binder-V6.pdf#page=20) · [PDF p21](https://media.team254.com/2023/10/90bc07c6-2023-Tech-Binder-V6.pdf#page=21)

**Published construction:** Intermediate superstructure states, reduced-precision transitions and a compliant laterator intake mode.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Move quickly while avoiding collisions and station impact loads.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A Cartesian-looking mechanism still needs a safe sequence through its intermediate states. Requiring every joint to settle precisely at every waypoint wastes time, while removing all intermediate conditions can create a collision. A compliant acquisition mode trades position stiffness for reduced impact, so its transition back to scoring control must be deliberate. Vision and odometry should supply a confidence-aware pose; the mechanical compliance is a complement to that estimate rather than evidence that accurate sensing is unnecessary.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Start transitions from unexpected interrupted states, test a station impact, and verify that the mechanism returns to a known scoring reference.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## OPR 2024: chassis and module geometry create the intake path

Version: 2024 pivoting shooter. [PDF p4](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/OPR24-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=4) · [PDF p6](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/OPR24-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=6) · [PDF p8](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/OPR24-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=8)

**Published construction:** Modified front module clearance; under-bumper conveyor; post-Newmarket aluminum side plates and added bracing.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Wide pickup, consistent centering and impact rigidity.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** An under-bumper path consumes the same volume as frame rails and module motors, so module orientation and mounting plates are part of the intake design. Increasing plate rigidity preserves compression but can transmit more collision load elsewhere. The documented event boundary should be retained: the stronger side plates and bracing were a precautionary update rather than necessarily the initial robot. Intake width is useful only if the full path can move off-center notes without trapping them at a module or frame corner.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test side pickup and corner impacts, then compare roller alignment and chassis squareness before and after the update.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## OPR 2024: pre-compression, differential spin and revised release angle

Version: 2024 pivoting shooter. [PDF p11](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/OPR24-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=11) · [PDF p13](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/OPR24-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=13) · [PDF p14](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/OPR24-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=14)

**Published construction:** Pre-compression contacts, independent left/right drives, low-backlash pivot; flywheels later tipped down 6°.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Consistent feed and greater useful shot range.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A flexible note can enter the same nominal wheel gap in different shapes. Pre-compression aims to control that shape before final acceleration. Independent side speeds then create spin, while mechanically linked upper/lower contacts preserve another aspect of consistency. A six-degree structural change alters the reachable trajectory envelope even if the control software is unchanged. Distinguish output speed, compression and release geometry when diagnosing misses: increasing RPM cannot necessarily compensate for a deformed or inconsistently presented note.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare shot distributions before and after the geometric revision with the same notes, recording entry deformation and wheel recovery.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: OPR 2024: pneumatic lift and an explicitly different disable behavior

## OPR 2024: pneumatic lift and an explicitly different disable behavior

Version: 2024 pivoting shooter. [PDF p16](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/OPR24-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=16)

**Published construction:** Dual pneumatic cylinders and revised double hook; single-acting valve retracts on loss of power.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Fast hanging and compatibility with a partner-loaded chain.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A pneumatic climber stores energy before the lift, reducing the need for a large electric winch during the final action. Available force depends on regulated pressure, piston area and the retracting-side rod area, while repeated actions consume finite stored air. The hook geometry must accommodate a chain already displaced by a partner. The described valve behavior is specific to this plumbing and control configuration; it should not become a generic assumption about all solenoids or an instruction to rely on an untested after-buzzer action.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test force and timing at the lowest expected pressure, including partner chain displacement and the actual disabled valve state.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: OPR 2024: adapt autonomous to whether a note is actually present
text:
## OPR 2024: adapt autonomous to whether a note is actually present

Version: 2024 pivoting shooter. [PDF p20](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/OPR24-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=20)

**Published construction:** Game-piece camera, drive-to-point correction, missing-note diversion and velocity-compensated aiming.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Avoid wasting autonomous time on absent or displaced notes.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** An intake with a large acquisition envelope becomes more useful when the path can correct toward the observed note. The controller must decide early enough that a failed attempt does not consume the rest of autonomous. A missing-note branch is a strategy choice tied to contested supply and partner routes, not simply a vision feature. The shot system also depends on current robot velocity and a stable angle reference. Database recommendations should include these feedback assumptions alongside the mechanical pickup.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Displace or remove expected notes and test diversion timing, partner-route safety and the resulting end pose.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: VORTEX: centered under-bumper acquisition
text:
## VORTEX: centered under-bumper acquisition

Version: VORTEX. [PDF p11](https://media.team254.com/2024/10/8f2607a0-2024-Tech-Binder.pdf#page=11)

**Published construction:** Mecanum front contact, kicker rollers and angled powered funneling wheels.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Accept side approaches and center notes without jamming.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A note arriving sideways or off-center should be translated toward the feeder before the shooter demands a repeatable entry state. Mecanum and angled contacts can supply that transverse velocity, but excess lateral force can fold or wedge the note. A stiff bumper and intake mount preserve the intended compression under defense. The correct performance measure includes successful ownership from the edge of the mouth, not only straight-on pickup at the center.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Map pickup across the mouth with deformed notes, oblique approaches and bumper impacts; observe the first region where motion stops.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: VORTEX: annular feed removes the intake-indexing heading constraint
text:
## VORTEX: annular feed removes the intake-indexing heading constraint

Version: VORTEX. [PDF p12](https://media.team254.com/2024/10/8f2607a0-2024-Tech-Binder.pdf#page=12) · [PDF p13](https://media.team254.com/2024/10/8f2607a0-2024-Tech-Binder.pdf#page=13)

**Published construction:** Two-direction annular feeder supplies a turret without returning it to the intake; 720° cable system.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Maintain goal tracking during acquisition and feeding.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The architectural benefit is not merely a large turret angle. Many turreted designs must rotate to an intake alignment before receiving a note, losing continuous tracking. An annular feed trades that delay for a larger guided path whose friction, seams and direction switching must be managed. Choosing the shorter route can reduce feed time, while a reversal must preserve piece state. The cable system makes the aiming envelope physically usable; without reliable wire guidance, the extra angular range is only a CAD possibility.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Feed at multiple turret headings including through a direction change; test note wear, guide friction and cable-chain operation near both limits.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## VORTEX: revised shooter separates feed and launch contacts

Version: VORTEX. [PDF p14](https://media.team254.com/2024/10/8f2607a0-2024-Tech-Binder.pdf#page=14)

**Published construction:** Second-revision quad-wheel shooter; staged feed rollers; asymmetrical wheels; sector-gear hood.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Controlled note entry and spin for a flatter useful trajectory.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The note’s flexible ring makes its entry orientation and deformation important to launch repeatability. A dedicated first stage can establish the approach before the high-speed wheels impart the final velocity and spin. Asymmetric contact can bias spin, but the resulting flight still needs empirical validation over wear and range. Hood backlash is an angular error that becomes more consequential at some distances than others. The revision label matters: a final shooter image must not silently stand in for an earlier competition version.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure entry deformation and shot dispersion with several note conditions; compare hood approaches from both directions and both feed routes.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

Passive trap-reaction wheels supply a structural contact during climbing, tying its geometry to the endgame sequence. The agent should explain those dependencies before recommending the package to a team that only needs one of its functions.

## VORTEX: rapid rope climb establishes trap height

Version: VORTEX. [PDF p16](https://media.team254.com/2024/10/8f2607a0-2024-Tech-Binder.pdf#page=16)

Gas springs can deploy the hooks while the winch retracts them under load. A rope path needs secure anchors, consistent winding and sufficient clearance as the robot swings. If retention relies on drivetrain or motor braking behavior, that exact power-off state should be validated rather than assumed. The trap sequence must preserve the reaction contact and note orientation throughout the lift.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test acquisition, lift, trap alignment and disable as one sequence with several chain heights and swing angles.

title: NOCTURNE: passive centering trades motor count for geometry
text:
## NOCTURNE: passive centering trades motor count for geometry

Version: NOCTURNE at Granite State. [PDF p10](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/ih64E84mBXtAJg7fKLBo7rgi5xM.pdf#page=10) · [Team explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/445350/82) · [Team explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/445350/95)

**Published construction:** Fast under-bumper rollers with passive wedges replacing an active-centering beta design.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reduce current while retaining useful acquisition.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A passive wedge can convert forward motion into centering without another motor, but requires the right approach velocity, contact friction and space for the note to move laterally. If a note is pinched against the wedge before it is captured, a faster roller can make the jam worse. The source represents the Granite State configuration, and a later team account describes impact failures and difficult repairs. The observed update is therefore part of the technical recommendation: a pickup can satisfy its contact objective while losing event value through poor service access.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test wide and oblique capture, then time a damaged roller replacement and verify alignment after repair.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## NOCTURNE: reuse a familiar joint and simplify the architecture

Version: NOCTURNE at Granite State. [PDF p3](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/ih64E84mBXtAJg7fKLBo7rgi5xM.pdf#page=3) · [PDF p6](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/ih64E84mBXtAJg7fKLBo7rgi5xM.pdf#page=6) · [PDF p7](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/ih64E84mBXtAJg7fKLBo7rgi5xM.pdf#page=7)

**Published construction:** Single-joint arm, paired planetary drives, chain final reduction and output-angle sensing.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reuse 2023 experience and preserve time before week 1.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A familiar joint can reduce the number of new mechanical and software problems, which matters when experienced students have graduated. It still needs a force-path and backlash review for its new payload. Multiple chain runs can distribute load but require matched tension so one does not carry nearly everything. A hard-stop shot gives a mechanically referenced fallback when vision or arm control fails, but repeated impact into the stop can change alignment. Schedule feasibility is a legitimate architecture criterion alongside reach and nominal speed.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure output repeatability under reversing load and after repeated hard-stop approaches; test the documented fallback with vision disabled.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: NOCTURNE: stage the note before launch while minimizing distal mass

## NOCTURNE: stage the note before launch while minimizing distal mass

Version: NOCTURNE at Granite State. [PDF p8](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/ih64E84mBXtAJg7fKLBo7rgi5xM.pdf#page=8) · [PDF p9](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/ih64E84mBXtAJg7fKLBo7rgi5xM.pdf#page=9)

**Published construction:** Eight launch wheels; lightweight staging rollers and low-friction guides integrated with the scorer.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Hold and preaccelerate without another storage mechanism.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A staging section can establish a repeatable note entry and prevent an uncontrolled piece from touching the flywheels prematurely. Using a smaller motor reduces moving mass only if it still supplies enough capture and feed force. The structure must resist both wheel vibration and arm acceleration; a flexible mount changes the launch angle even with correct encoder readings. A grippy stage and low-friction guides serve different purposes: one supplies drive while the other avoids wasting that effort. Test the full transfer at operating speed rather than assuming more grip everywhere is better.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure note-entry timing, launch dispersion and structure vibration with new and worn notes while the arm is moving.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

text:
## NOCTURNE: the real field exposed calibration and fallback needs

Version: NOCTURNE at Granite State. [PDF p12](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/ih64E84mBXtAJg7fKLBo7rgi5xM.pdf#page=12) · [PDF p13](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/ih64E84mBXtAJg7fKLBo7rgi5xM.pdf#page=13) · [Team explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/445350/82) · [Team explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/445350/95)

**Published construction:** Pose-based shot map, motion lookahead and automatic intake stop after note detection.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Aim through brief vision loss and avoid accidental extra possession.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A consistent pose estimate can still be systematically wrong if the practice target or camera geometry is wrong. Calibrating a lookup table against an inaccurate practice field can make reliable local shots fail at an event. A safe fallback should use a mechanically repeatable pose with a validated close shot, rather than trusting the same mistaken distance model. The fixed under-bumper intake also creates a possession-control requirement because it cannot simply retract away from a second piece. Mechanical geometry and sensor timing must be verified together.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Validate against measured field geometry, remove expected vision input, and test closely spaced notes for unintended second-piece capture.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Validate wheel arrangement and compression in CAD, then test dispersion and elevator deflection across the intended scoring range.

## ROTI: one lift creates scoring height and endgame capability

Version: ROTI. [PDF p5](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1JueptXU9TRB6N2dDGX-fZ-d9fCz3nMKs/view#page=5) · [PDF p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1JueptXU9TRB6N2dDGX-fZ-d9fCz3nMKs/view#page=8) · [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1JueptXU9TRB6N2dDGX-fZ-d9fCz3nMKs/view#page=9)

**Published construction:** Continuous rope lift with overextending carriage; passive lower hooks retain the chain after initial lift.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Use one shooter for speaker, amp and trap.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Moving the shooter upward changes its release geometry and can improve defended shot access, while stowing preserves travel routes under the stage. That broad capability costs raised mass and a multi-state handoff. The passive lower hooks are central to the climb: they take over the suspension load so the elevator can extend again for trap scoring. Without that load transfer, the same actuator cannot independently hold the robot and reposition the scorer. This is an architectural sequence rather than an elevator plus an unrelated climber.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Verify passive-hook engagement before re-extension; test full-height stability and stowed route clearance with the actual scorer mass.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## FIREFLY: wheel stiffness is part of end-effector accuracy

Version: FIREFLY. [PDF p10](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/5VYfconlxrh4QdiOcvuLGWunsv1.pdf#page=10) · [PDF p11](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/5VYfconlxrh4QdiOcvuLGWunsv1.pdf#page=11) · [Team explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/502317/5)

**Published construction:** Custom Grip Lock hubs, lowered Mk4-C base and later lower drive gearing.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reduce tire flex and preserve a stiff floor-to-tool reference.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Wheel compliance permits the chassis to rotate relative to the carpet even when the frame and elevator are stiff. The resulting angular error becomes a larger displacement at an elevated tool, so a tire-hub change can improve L4 placement without changing the wrist. A low frame and ballast distribution address another component of the same stability problem. The gearing revision also changes acceleration and braking behavior; it needs drive retuning with the real mechanism load. Do not treat a module model or a free speed as a complete explanation of placement repeatability.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure tool-tip displacement under known lateral load and during stopping, separating tire deflection from lift deflection.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: FIREFLY: short lift and low-mounted carriage actuators
text:
## FIREFLY: short lift and low-mounted carriage actuators

Version: FIREFLY. [PDF p8](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/5VYfconlxrh4QdiOcvuLGWunsv1.pdf#page=8) · [PDF p12](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/5VYfconlxrh4QdiOcvuLGWunsv1.pdf#page=12)

**Published construction:** Single-stage counterbalanced lift; thin-wall tube; algae, coral and arm drives mounted low on carriage.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Low moving center of gravity and direct piece delivery.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Remoting the roller drives removes mass from the far end of the arm while keeping it on the lift carriage. That reduces one component of arm inertia without eliminating the carriage mass that the lift must accelerate. A single-stage lift can simplify guidance but requires the arm to supply the remaining reach and orientation. Counterbalance reduces gravity demand, while belt tension and routing still determine tracking and friction. The integration goal is a useful task sequence with no wait for piece delivery, rather than a collection of independently fast axes.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure lift current and tool settling during combined motion; verify belt tension and direct-handoff clearance at every relevant pose.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## FIREFLY: sideways orientation while maintaining coral ownership

Version: FIREFLY. [PDF p14](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/5VYfconlxrh4QdiOcvuLGWunsv1.pdf#page=14)

**Published construction:** Sideways reorienting belt, compliant tube rollers, independent roller drives and twisted-belt transmission.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Direct handoff or controlled L1 without staging the coral.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A sideways belt gives the tube a deliberate transverse velocity rather than relying only on passive wedges. The remaining contacts must keep ownership while that reorientation happens; an unconstrained gap can erase the advantage. Separate roller drives permit holding a tube for L1 or continuing into the end effector, but create more state choices and sensor requirements. Twisted and bent belts solve an off-axis power-routing problem, while adding tracking, wear and alignment concerns. Their tension cannot be chosen solely for torque transmission if the belt also participates in piece contact.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Film diagonal and lengthwise entries through both L1 and handoff branches, then repeat after belt wear and an intake impact.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## FIREFLY: dedicated floor-algae route integrates with climb

Version: FIREFLY. [PDF p13](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/5VYfconlxrh4QdiOcvuLGWunsv1.pdf#page=13)

**Published construction:** Counter-rotating floor-algae rollers; reinforced printed bevel gears; three-piece jackshaft around climb packaging.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Acquire algae and deliver it to the arm without subsystem interference.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A dedicated floor pickup lets the main end effector specialize in retention and scoring rather than reaching a difficult carpet pose. That value must exceed the added mass and handoff complexity. Segmenting the jackshaft can make assembly possible around another subsystem, but every joint adds an alignment and torque-transfer interface. Printed bevel gears need stable bearing support and an appropriate tooth load; a successful material in another mechanism does not certify this one. The pathway should remain useful if the climb is damaged, consistent with the robot’s stated degraded-operation objective.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test floor acquisition and handoff while climb is stowed, partially deployed and disabled; inspect bevel alignment under peak capture load.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## FIREFLY: internal coral grip and algae torque selected by test

Version: FIREFLY. [PDF p15](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/5VYfconlxrh4QdiOcvuLGWunsv1.pdf#page=15) · [Team explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/502317/11)

**Published construction:** Internal coral gripping; compliant placement geometry; shared tool also acquires and scores algae.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Control both pieces while keeping moving structure light.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Gripping inside a tube changes the reference surface and can leave the outside clearer for placement. It still needs a controlled release and enough compliance to tolerate the branch without wedging the tool. Algae retention is a different torque problem: the wheel must deform and hold a soft sphere rather than simply spin at the desired acquisition speed. A practical way to choose the ratio is to measure the required final-shaft torque, then check speed and motor current under that load. This is more informative than selecting a reduction from a famous robot without matching its compression and geometry.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure algae pull-in torque and holding current, then test coral release with intentional branch misalignment and the same worn contacts.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## FIREFLY: custom cycloidal reduction is an iterative capability

Version: FIREFLY. [PDF p17](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/5VYfconlxrh4QdiOcvuLGWunsv1.pdf#page=17)

**Published construction:** 23:1 dual-disc cycloidal; hardened steel discs; rolling pins; team reports about 0.3° backlash.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Compact, lightweight low-backlash joint drive.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A cycloidal gearbox trades ordinary spur stages for a shaped eccentric load path with multiple contacts. Opposed discs can reduce dynamic imbalance, but machining accuracy, pin support and eccentric bearings still control vibration, efficiency and backlash. The reported backlash is a team result for its design and measurement conditions. It should not be assumed for a copied outline made with a different process. This is a mature, revised manufacturing capability, so its adoption cost includes inspection, heat treatment and assembly knowledge rather than just CAD availability.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Characterize output backlash, temperature and efficiency under the intended reversing load, and inspect contact wear after repeated shock cycles.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

text:
## AURELIA: package the base around two different clearances

Version: AURELIA. [PDF p4](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=4) · [PDF p5](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=5)

**Published construction:** 28-inch square chassis; X2i elevator-side modules and X2t intake-side modules; custom lowering spacers.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Motor protection, low chassis and intake gearbox clearance.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Choosing different module orientations within one drivebase is a packaging solution rather than a reason to recommend mixed modules universally. A motor placed inside can protect the elevator-side envelope while an outward placement can free an intake drive path. The lowering hardware must preserve module stiffness and ground clearance under a loaded, accelerating robot. Low mass is helpful, but the more relevant quantity for fast reef approach is the loaded center of mass and its motion as the shoulder and elevator change state. Include bumper and battery interfaces in the same model.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Sweep the complete intake/elevator envelope against each module; measure clearance and wheel unloading through aggressive scoring transitions.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: AURELIA: separate coral and algae contacts on a shared axis
text:
## AURELIA: separate coral and algae contacts on a shared axis

Version: AURELIA. [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=7) · [PDF p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=8) · [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=9) · [Team explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/500435/131)

**Published construction:** Coaxial intake pivots; separate deployment reductions; shared roller drive; bilateral transfer tubes.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** The team explicitly ties this intake choice to horizontal L1 placement, alongside concerns about a separate centering/indexing system.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Sharing an axis does not make these one generic intake. Each piece needs a different contact geometry, and the dedicated L1 action depends on their relative positions. Driving both sides helps prevent an arm from twisting out of phase during asymmetric contact. A common roller drive saves a motor and packaging but couples the desired surface speeds of the two pickup functions. The useful retrieval target is the entire relative geometry and state sequence: which surface acquires, which guides, and which constrains the coral during release. A lone roller photo cannot explain the L1 performance.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Film the complete L1 cycle from first floor contact through release; vary coral orientation, reef occupancy and approach angle.

**Limits:** Team reply reports difficult horizontal approaches beyond about 45 degrees, extensive practice and late-season durability work. Successful match execution is not proof of effortless any-orientation pickup.

## AURELIA: center coral before a direct handoff

Version: AURELIA. [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=9)

**Published construction:** Flex upper rollers, grippy lower rollers, about 0.125-inch coral compression and proximity detection.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Center coral and hand directly into the end effector.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A low-compression pickup can reduce the force required to accept an awkwardly oriented tube, but it leaves less traction margin when the surfaces are dirty or the coral is wedged against another piece. Centering before transfer reduces the number of states the end effector must solve. A direct handoff avoids an intermediate tray, while demanding that the receiving geometry arrive at the right position before the piece loses its previous constraint. Sensor placement should identify the handoff state, rather than simply report that some portion of a long tube is nearby.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test slow, diagonal and multi-piece approaches; observe whether detection occurs before, during or after reliable ownership transfers.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## AURELIA: four-stage lift on a rotating shoulder

Version: AURELIA. [PDF p6](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=6) · [PDF p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=10) · [PDF p11](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=11)

**Published construction:** Shoulder-supported four-stage continuous elevator; internal HTD belts; interlocking extended-stage stops.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Compact packaging with stiffness at scoring height.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The shoulder changes both the lift’s direction and its center-of-mass path. A multi-stage lift can reach high while stowing short, but introduces more interfaces that can deflect or develop play. Hard stops that engage at extension can add stiffness where the mechanism otherwise has the least overlap; they must not produce damaging impacts at operating speed. The carriage’s integrated gearbox reduces redundant structure while making belt access and service sequencing important. In the alliance role described by the user, much of the robot’s value comes from low scoring and algae, yet its high reach still supplies capability and tactical flexibility.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure tip error and settling after shoulder/elevator transitions, including side acceleration and partial rather than only full extension.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## AURELIA: differential wrist and independently driven rollers

Version: AURELIA. [PDF p12](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=12) · [PDF p13](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Y2ooTZMBNoViMZ6R4wYOkom1mhIIqF-R/view?usp=sharing#page=13)

**Published construction:** Printed bevel differential; paired 61.6:1 drives; independent coral rollers; front algae pinch wheels.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reorient coral while keeping the moving end effector compact.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A differential combines two motor coordinates into two output motions. That can package orientation control densely, but means a joint motion may require both motors and leave less authority for the other axis at the same instant. Printed bevel gears need controlled bearing alignment and a stiffness model; backlash at a small output stage becomes placement error at the coral tip. Independent roller contacts can change tube orientation before release, which is particularly valuable for intentional L1 placement and stacking. The same hardware can support very different alliance jobs, so high-level capability must be separated from the task actually assigned in a match.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Command combined wrist motions under realistic piece load; measure output backlash and horizontal-coral placement consistency across L1 pile heights.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reuse primary joints while controlling the hanging geometry.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A shared-joint climb saves dedicated structure only if the primary system can react the new loads. Capturing one cage tube is different from supporting the robot after the cage rotates; the lower reaction point and position of the chain relative to the robot’s center of mass determine the motion. The sliding support permits that geometry to change rather than requiring a single fixed pivot to solve every phase. Reuse also couples faults: a damaged shoulder, end effector or intake latch can affect climb. Record the support contact explicitly instead of reducing the design to “uses its arm to climb.”

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test cage swing and off-center capture, inspect every reaction contact, and verify retention after power is removed.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## OPR 2025: floating capture and protected pivot drive

Version: 2025 REEFSCAPE robot. [PDF p7](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/OPR25-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=7) · [PDF p8](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/OPR25-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=8)

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Tolerant coral pickup with motors protected in the frame.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Coaxial power transmission lets a roller remain driven as the intake pivots without a long changing-center belt run. The floating contact accommodates an awkward tube orientation while the lower contact keeps it moving into the robot. Synchronizing both sides resists twist, but an impact can still concentrate load at the polycarbonate-to-aluminum joint. Large clamps distribute this force and retain the bearing as the plate flexes. Automatic retraction protects the collector only after the sensor has confirmed that the tube is safely inside.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test diagonal pickup, asymmetric loading and capture-triggered retraction; inspect bearing retention following a side impact.

## OPR 2025: independent straightening drives and staged cradle sensing

Version: 2025 REEFSCAPE robot. [PDF p9](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/OPR25-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=9) · [PDF p10](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/OPR25-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=10) · [PDF p11](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/OPR25-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=11) · [PDF p12](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/OPR25-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=12)

**Published construction:** Independently driven straightener sides; current-triggered reversal; two-sensor cradle with anti-bounce step.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Align coral and recover jams before handoff.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Independent sides permit relative slip or reversal instead of forcing both ends of a tube forward at the same speed. Current sensing can identify resistance, but must distinguish a normal capture transient from a persistent jam. The cradle then changes the problem from continuous alignment to a discrete known handoff position. A stop lip and anti-bounce feature control longitudinal motion, while cutouts provide room for the receiving gripper. Excessively constraining the tube at the same time as the gripper closes can create a new jam, so the handoff sequence matters as much as the tray shape.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Feed tubes at skewed angles, tune jam detection against false triggers, and test receiver clearance during an interrupted handoff.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## OPR 2025: reduce moving inertia without losing algae grip

Version: 2025 REEFSCAPE robot. [PDF p13](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/OPR25-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=13) · [PDF p14](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/OPR25-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=14)

**Published construction:** Formed-sheet arm replaced tubing; lighter geared gripper drive; remoted motor; velocity-matched coral ejection.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reduce mass and pivot moment while keeping functional grip.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Removing mass far from the pivot reduces inertia more effectively than removing the same mass near the axis. A remoted motor achieves that while adding a transmission whose backlash and compliance must be controlled. Formed sheet can provide a stiff section with low mass if the flanges and joints react the actual loads. Matching ejection to chassis motion can reduce unwanted relative velocity at release, but requires consistent roller surface speed and piece position. It is a coordinated robot motion, not a passive property of the gripper.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure tip settling and grip under acceleration; test scoring while approaching and backing away at several speeds.

title: UNDERTOW: short-cycle gearing and low mass placement
text:
## UNDERTOW: short-cycle gearing and low mass placement

Version: UNDERTOW. [PDF p12](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=12)

**Published construction:** 29.5-inch square base; low 3×1 frame; X2i modules geared about 13.2 ft/s free speed.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Favor acceleration and grip over long-run top speed.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** For a short reef cycle, acceleration, braking and repeatable final alignment can matter more than a higher unloaded top speed. Lower gearing increases available wheel torque but does not guarantee traction; wheel compound, normal load and current limits still bound acceleration. A broad low base helps resist tipping while the elevator changes height, but occupies more traffic space. The useful comparison uses the actual route and raised mechanism state rather than a module specification on its own.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure complete reef-to-supply cycle time, stopping error and wheel unloading with the elevator at representative positions.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: UNDERTOW: floating continuous rollers and four-bar deployment
text:
## UNDERTOW: floating continuous rollers and four-bar deployment

Version: UNDERTOW. [PDF p13](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=13)

**Published construction:** Foam/silicone continuous rollers, floating front plate, rubber-band dead-zone belts and four-bar deployment.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Admit longways coral and yield during collisions.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A continuous compliant surface can avoid the discrete kicks caused by spaced wheels, while a floating roller accommodates the changing cross-section presented by a tube approaching diagonally. Rubber bands bridge regions where neither main roller can maintain ownership. They also introduce wear, tracking and tension variables, so their role should be tested rather than treated as decorative assistance. The four-bar positions the deployed pickup without requiring its pivot at the very front of the chassis. Copy the contact geometry and trajectory together: substituting a single pivot can change both bumper clearance and handoff.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Approach coral at a grid of angles, measure uninterrupted contact, and repeat after a wall impact and belt replacement.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: UNDERTOW: flatten and index before handing off
text:
## UNDERTOW: flatten and index before handing off

Version: UNDERTOW. [PDF p14](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=14) · [PDF p15](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=15)

**Published construction:** Eight compliant/star wheels; guide wedges, flattening yoke and beam breaks; separate steep station funnel.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Create a repeatable handoff from either source.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Ground and station pickup arrive with different velocities and orientations. A common indexer lets the end effector see a smaller set of input states, but the funnel and pickup must not feed incompatible positions. Wedges and a flattening wheel create deliberate constraints; if they constrain too many dimensions at once, the tube can wedge rather than align. Sensors should identify the indexed state before the receiver moves. The station funnel adds redundancy and autonomous options, so its value depends on how much extra envelope and mass it costs alongside floor acquisition.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare handoff time and jam rate from both sources with skewed and bouncing arrivals; test the full state sequence after a missed detection.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: UNDERTOW: fast continuous elevator
text:
## UNDERTOW: fast continuous elevator

Version: UNDERTOW. [PDF p16](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=16)

**Published construction:** Two-stage internal-belt lift; two X60s; welded support frame; team reports roughly 0.3-second full travel.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reach scoring heights rapidly and maintain stiffness.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A fast travel number does not include settling, alignment or release. Internal belts protect the drive path but make access, tensioning and inspection more important. The support frame must react lateral inertia from the raised wrist as well as the elevator’s own acceleration. If the system reaches height quickly but sways outside the coral-placement tolerance, the useful cycle has not improved. A matched recommendation needs carriage mass, output stiffness, profile constraints and a maintenance plan rather than only belt width and motor count.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure time until the coral tip enters and stays within scoring tolerance, not merely until the encoder reaches its height setpoint.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: UNDERTOW: Flying V compliance and an L1 pass-through
text:
## UNDERTOW: Flying V compliance and an L1 pass-through

Version: UNDERTOW. [PDF p18](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=18) · [PDF p19](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=19)

**Published construction:** Wrist-mounted compliant coral roller, pipe-aligning Flying V, cam-controlled rear hoop and shared algae drive.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Fast branch placement with controlled piece handoff.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Mechanical alignment can absorb residual chassis error by guiding the end effector relative to the actual pipe. It must do so without pushing the tube into a trapped configuration or transmitting a large side load into the wrist. The movable hoop illustrates why the handoff and L1 scoring states differ: a stop that is necessary to receive coral can obstruct the intended exit. Sharing a motor between piece contacts reduces moving mass but couples their speed and torque requirements. The complete mechanism includes the cam state and sensing, not just the front roller.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Map tolerated lateral and angular pipe error, test handoff against L1 pass-through, and repeat with a worn wheel and occupied nearby branches.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: UNDERTOW: capture first, then winch the robot under the cage
text:
## UNDERTOW: capture first, then winch the robot under the cage

Version: UNDERTOW. [PDF p17](https://media.team254.com/2025/09/985607eb-2025-Tech-Binder-254.pdf#page=17)

**Published construction:** Powered roller claw, passive latch, gas-spring deployment and low-mounted ratcheting winch.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Acquire a cage quickly and retain suspension after disable.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Separating capture from lifting allows the capture wheels to optimize entry while the winch carries the robot load. The latch and cage reaction surfaces must take over reliably before the wheels stop providing traction. Remoting the winch lowers mass but lengthens the tension path and adds rope-routing concerns. A deep-climb recommendation should identify acquisition tolerance, how the cage rotates, where the chain ends relative to the robot’s center of mass, and the load path after power is removed.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test swinging-cage acquisition, transition from powered rollers to latch, and power-off retention with the actual rope routing.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: SPECTRE: base and module revision at Championship
text:
## SPECTRE: base and module revision at Championship

Version: SPECTRE. [PDF p5](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bjl1LJRS1vXOiLeVq6HdaQw0rmdQOUhk/view#page=5)

**Published construction:** District Mk4i modules changed to prototype Mk5 at Worlds; ballast placement also changed.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Low center of gravity and short-cycle maneuverability.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A module swap is a robot version, even if the scoring architecture looks unchanged. Saving module weight can be reinvested as low ballast rather than removed from the robot, changing traction and stability differently from a simple weight reduction. A wide tread and different enclosure can alter friction, debris protection and maintenance. Retuning drive and autonomous behavior is part of the mechanical change: old acceleration and feedforward assumptions should not be carried over without measurements. The database should name the competition stage associated with each configuration.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare module slip, current and stopping repeatability before and after the change with the actual ballast and bumper package.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: SPECTRE: remote power at an integrated pivot
text:
## SPECTRE: remote power at an integrated pivot

Version: SPECTRE. [PDF p6](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bjl1LJRS1vXOiLeVq6HdaQw0rmdQOUhk/view#page=6) · [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bjl1LJRS1vXOiLeVq6HdaQw0rmdQOUhk/view#page=9)

**Published construction:** Separate three-X60 shoulder and extension gearboxes; dead-axle pivot; two-stage cascade arm.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Fast motion with a low stowed center of gravity and serviceable arm.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Keeping heavy actuators near the base reduces distal inertia and lets the arm respond without carrying all its drive mass at the tip. The price is a more complicated transmission across the pivot and through the telescope. A coaxial extension drive must preserve tension and alignment over the shoulder’s range. A large shared pivot can support stiffness and removal, but its clamps and end plugs become critical load interfaces. Motor count alone does not explain speed: the arm’s inertia, reduction, current limits and acceleration profile determine whether it can move quickly without rocking the chassis.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure end-point settling after simultaneous pivot and extension; test removal/reinstallation repeatability and chain tension over the full range.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: SPECTRE: acquire, orient and score with one end mechanism
text:
## SPECTRE: acquire, orient and score with one end mechanism

Version: SPECTRE. [PDF p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bjl1LJRS1vXOiLeVq6HdaQw0rmdQOUhk/view#page=8)

**Published construction:** Vertical and horizontal roller sets; four CANrange sensors; reversible front/back handoff and scoring.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Serve coral and algae tasks with the same manipulator.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Combining acquisition and scoring avoids a separate transfer interface, but makes the moving assembly larger and creates competing contact requirements. Coral has to be oriented differently for branches and L1; algae needs enough compliant pinch to stay captured during rapid motion. Multiple sensors can distinguish piece position and direction, provided their views remain reliable for both geometries. Front/back scoring reduces chassis rotation when the software chooses a sensible approach. The architecture should be assessed by complete cycle time and reach under defense, not by the number of available poses.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test front/back coral scoring, intentional horizontal L1 placement and algae capture with the same rollers after wear.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## SPECTRE: moving climb carriage manages the hanging center

Version: SPECTRE. [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bjl1LJRS1vXOiLeVq6HdaQw0rmdQOUhk/view#page=7) · [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bjl1LJRS1vXOiLeVq6HdaQw0rmdQOUhk/view#page=9)

**Published construction:** Powered one-bar cage capture; carriage slides along arm; shoulder lifts; extension locks to bumper structure.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Balance under the chain while reusing the main arm.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The carriage is not just a convenient mount. Its translation changes where the cage pulls relative to the robot’s mass, allowing a controlled transition into suspension. The shoulder then supplies the lifting work and the arm lock supplies a post-match retention path. Those are separate functions and should be recorded separately. Reusing the arm reduces dedicated hardware but raises its required load and reliability. Any recommendation needs the actual cage contact, latch, shoulder and lock sequence rather than assuming that a strong scoring arm can safely substitute for a complete climber.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Capture at several swing angles, verify carriage travel under load, and test power-off retention through the intended bumper lock.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

title: SPECTRE: automate approach choice and L1 placement
text:
## SPECTRE: automate approach choice and L1 placement

Version: SPECTRE. [PDF p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bjl1LJRS1vXOiLeVq6HdaQw0rmdQOUhk/view#page=10)

**Published construction:** Automatic front/back reef choice; level/side selected by driver; distinct base/top L1 states.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Remove repeated alignment work from the driver.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Choosing the nearest face or easiest orientation can save time, but the shortest geometric route is not always the least congested or the most valuable remaining target. L1 stacking creates an occupancy problem as well as a pose problem: a fixed placement height is insufficient once previous coral changes the landing surface. The driver still needs strategic control over task and side, with software handling repeatable motion. A mechanism recommendation should include the sensors, pose references and operator choices required to realize its cycle advantage.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test automatic choices near boundaries between faces and with populated L1; verify deliberate driver override and recovery after a failed release.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.
